input.rationale: Attempted the next increment - configuration events aimed at an existing serving member (so a voter can be demoted and re-promoted) - and it failed in a way worth recording rather than hiding. With application lag present, aiming a JointImplicit change at a serving member made the harness panic with 'config is already joint' inside applyConfChange: a node applies a joint-entering change while its own tracked configuration is still joint, because the auto-leave it should have applied first is exactly the kind of entry the lag event holds back. That is the target's documented contract for an invalid configuration change (the application must apply each change in the order its log provides, and a change that enters joint while joint is invalid), so the failure is a harness modelling error, not a target defect: the harness applied a change out of the order the contract assumes at that node. I reverted to the last known-good revision (configuration events aimed at the joining node 4 only, JointImplicit half the time, lag, restarts, witness) and confirmed locally that it runs again and reproduces the executed counters exactly (elections=470, proposals=461, conf_change_proposals=262, restarts=429, unapplied_conf_change_states=48, stalled_states=0, violations=0), so no experiment is requested this turn. The failure does open a real, sourced follow-up worth pursuing next: with Config.DisableConfChangeValidation left at its default, the leader's propose-time check is explicitly best-effort against its own possibly stale configuration, so a joint-entering change can enter the log while some lagging node is still joint; the question is whether a permitted sequence can leave a node unable to apply a committed change except by panicking, i.e. whether the lag/demotion ordering is bounded by application duties alone or by anything the target enforces.

investigations.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
investigations.hypothesis: The panic is the documented consequence of an application that applies committed entries out of order or of a proposal that the leader's best-effort check allowed through while its configuration was stale; the target's own duty is only that the application applies entries in log order, so a permitted history exists in which a node is forced to apply a joint-entering change while joint, and the question is whether the propose-time check (or the auto-leave path) bounds it in every case.
investigations.discriminator: Build a three-voter cluster with AutoLeave/JointImplicit, hold one follower's application back (so its leave-joint entry stays unapplied while the leader is non-joint again), propose a second joint-entering change, and observe whether the withheld follower, once its application catches up in log order, applies a joint-entering change while its tracker is joint - and whether the leader's propose-time validation had refused or rewritten that change. Compare with the control where the follower's application keeps up.

investigations.question: In this snapshot, ReadOnlySafe confirmation is count-based rather than commit-index-based (read_only.go addRequest/recvAck/maybeAdvance/heartbeatCtx with confirmedReads, driven from stepLeader MsgHeartbeatResp and sendMsgReadIndexResponse). Which conditions establish that a released ReadState carries an index at least as new as the commit index at the moment the request was admitted, and what happens to still-unconfirmed reads when the leader's term changes (reset() rebuilds readOnly) or when the leader is a fresh leader that has not yet committed an entry in its term (pendingReadIndexMessages)?
investigations.hypothesis: A released read index is never smaller than the commit index recorded at admission of that read request, because positions are monotonic counts and acks are per-voter maxima; the open risk is a lost completion (request dropped by reset/term change) rather than a stale index.
investigations.discriminator: Drive a real 3-node cluster in one process: elect a leader, admit a read request (MsgReadIndex via Step), delay only MsgHeartbeatResp so no quorum ack exists yet, then remove the leader (isolate) and elect a new leader that commits an entry. Deliver the delayed heartbeat responses to the stale leader and record every ReadState and every dropped request. Expected if the count-based claim holds: no ReadState is emitted whose Index is below the commit index at admission; expected counter-shape: an emitted ReadState with a too-small Index (stale read) or a request that is silently never answered after the leader's term changed (lost completion).

gaps.question: Is an unconfirmed ReadIndex request answered, dropped, or answered with a stale index when the leader loses its term between admission and quorum acknowledgement, and which of those outcomes is observable from the ReadState stream?

investigations.question: hup() refuses to campaign whenever hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true, i.e. whenever any entry in (applied, committed] is an EntryConfChange/EntryConfChangeV2, and promotable() additionally vetoes campaign while an unstable or in-progress snapshot exists. No existing test references hasUnappliedConfChanges directly. Which permitted histories leave a node with committed-but-unapplied configuration entries, and can such a node campaign with a voter set that does not include its own committed configuration (for example after restoring a snapshot, after ReadIndex-style lag in application, or when the application rejects a config change by zeroing NodeId)?
investigations.hypothesis: The guard is a deliberate safety measure (campaign only with an applied configuration) and is correct for the paths it covers, but its interaction with (a) applied<committed gaps created by the application, (b) MsgTimeoutNow-triggered campaigning, and (c) restore/bootstrap paths is untested and may either block a legal transfer or admit a campaign with a stale voter set.
investigations.discriminator: Construct a voter whose storage holds a committed EntryConfChangeV2 that the application has not applied (Config.Applied below committed) and whose stored ConfState predates it, then (i) tick into an election timeout and (ii) deliver MsgTimeoutNow, and read back whether it becomes candidate, which voter IDs it addresses in the MsgVote/MsgPreVote messages, and which quorum quorum.VoteResult uses; the alternative outcome to distinguish is a campaign that proceeds despite the unapplied change, or a permanent inability to campaign after the application refuses the change.

gaps.question: With a committed-but-unapplied conf change in the log, does the node refrain from campaigning (and if so, is a later campaign possible once application catches up), and which voter set would a campaign use if it did proceed?

investigations.question: The campaign guard is verified to suppress a MsgTimeoutNow-triggered campaign when the transferee has a committed-but-unapplied conf change (CheckRun 238d3a23d8624c438b85ec18f90a7b2b events 0-2). Which observable sequence follows for a requested leadership transfer whose transferee lags application: does the leader keep sending MsgTimeoutNow/MsgApp until tickHeartbeat aborts the transfer at the election timeout, can the cluster still make progress through the existing leader in the meantime (proposals dropped while leadTransferee != None), and is a later transfer possible once the transferee's application catches up? This is the bounded-liveness side of the same guard, where a duty the leader explicitly accepted (transfer) cannot complete and the leader also refuses proposals.
investigations.hypothesis: The transfer neither completes nor deadlocks: the transferee refuses to campaign while the conf change is unapplied, the leader keeps proposing the transfer (and drops new proposals) until its election timeout elapses, then abortLeaderTransfer() clears leadTransferee and proposals resume, so the cost is bounded by one election timeout and the transfer can be retried after the transformer catches up.
investigations.discriminator: In one process, elect a 3-node leader, give the transferee a committed-but-unapplied conf-change entry (applied < committed) via its storage/HardState and Config.Applied, call TransferLeader to it, then tick the leader past its election timeout and record: whether MsgTimeoutNow was sent, whether MsgProp is rejected with ErrProposalDropped while leadTransferee != None, whether leadTransferee is cleared after the timeout, and whether a second TransferLeader attempt after applying the entry completes with the transferee campaigning at term+1. Expected if the claim holds: transfer aborted within one election timeout, proposals accepted again afterwards, second attempt succeeding after application catches up; the alternative to distinguish is a forever-pending transfer (leadTransferee never cleared or proposals permanently dropped) or a transfer that completes with a stale voter set.

investigations.question: The two answered questions and the transfer probe all exercise single, hand-built prefixes: one conf-change entry with applied lag, one read admission followed by one term change, one requested transfer. Which safety relationships survive a randomized sequence of permitted events produced by the snapshot's own producers - elections, proposals, configuration changes (simple and joint), partitions and recovery, compaction and leadership transfer - under the invariants the implementation itself relies on: at most one leader per term, no two nodes ever committing different entries at the same index, no node's committed index regressing, applied never exceeding committed, and every committed entry staying committed after a leader change? The aim is to look for a source-grounded counterexample to a safety property rather than to confirm the documented conservative behaviors already established.
investigations.hypothesis: No counterexample exists among these invariants for the exercised event set, because the decisions that justify commitment and leadership are quorum-intersecting under both simple and joint configurations, and the probes already show the campaign and read paths being conservative rather than permissive; a counterexample, if the sweep finds one, would have to come from a path where a decision is taken under a configuration that does not intersect the configuration used to commit the entries it relies on.
investigations.discriminator: Randomized in-process sweep over the repository's own network and storage helpers with a fixed seed set, extended as follows for the unanswered gap. (1) Configuration events: with the same probability mass as proposals, inject a ConfChangeV2 on the current leader - alternating a learner add/remove, a voter add, a voter remove, and a two-change proposal that enters a joint configuration via ConfChangeTransitionJointImplicit, plus a follow-up zero-change proposal to leave it - and, unlike the previous case, apply what is committed as an application would: for each committed entry of type EntryConfChange/EntryConfChangeV2 call applyConfChange with the unmarshalled ConfChangeV2 (including the documented rejection form that zeroes NodeId) before advancing the applied index, so the node's tracked configuration actually changes. (2) Restart events: for a random node, re-create the raft instance from a MemoryStorage holding that node's persisted entries and hard state plus a ConfState the harness passes explicitly (via CreateSnapshot's cs parameter or an ApplySnapshot carrying it), because the previous turn established that MemoryStorage never updates the configuration itself; then continue the sweep with the re-created instance and check the same four invariants, adding that the restarted node's configuration and committed index are consistent with what it had persisted. (3) Liveness witness for the guard: after any event that leaves the current configuration's voter set with a committed-but-unapplied conf change at a majority of nodes, record whether any voter can still campaign and be elected, and whether a leader remains. The discriminators are the same four violation events plus a new event for a restarted node whose configuration or committed index contradicts its persisted state, and a summary event reporting how many configuration and restart events ran; absence over the fixed seed set stays a holds-only result.

knowledge.assertion: a restarted instance adopts the configuration from Storage.InitialState's ConfState, which MemoryStorage only changes when the caller supplies one

gaps.question: The executed sweep covered elections, proposals, ticks, isolate/recover, TransferLeader and persist/apply cycles, but not the configuration changes (simple and joint) and node restarts that the registered discriminator named. Do the four checked invariants still hold once ConfChangeV2 proposals (including joint transitions and learner promotions) and restarts of a node from its persisted MemoryStorage are included in the randomized event set, and does the campaign guard's applied-lag condition ever leave a live cluster without an electable voter in that wider set?
